description:
Gurdwara Choa Sahib — its name meaning the "gurdwara of the exalted spring" — stands at the northern edge of the great sixteenth-century *Rohtas Fort*, a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Jhelum, close to the fort's Talaqi gate. It commemorates a tradition of *Guru Nanak* (1469–1539): Sikhs hold that the Guru, travelling with his companion *Bhai Mardana* during the fourth of his great journeys (*udasis*) and having spent forty days at the nearby *Tilla Jogian*, came to this waterless tract in the heat of summer. When Bhai Mardana lamented his thirst, the Guru is said to have struck the ground with his staff and moved a stone, causing a natural spring to well up — the *choa* that gives the shrine its name. A further Sikh legend relates that Sher Shah Suri, builder of Rohtas Fort, thrice attempted to divert the spring uphill to supply his stronghold, and thrice his engineers failed. The first commemorative structure, with a *sarovar* (sacred tank) and a place for the recitation of the *Guru Granth Sahib*, is attributed to Charat Singh; the present building dates from 1834 and was commissioned by *Maharaja Ranjit Singh*. Long neglected after the Partition of 1947, the gurdwara was reopened to pilgrims around the time of Guru Nanak's 550th birth anniversary in 2019, and from 2020 a diaspora Sikh organisation undertook its rehabilitation and restoration.

Iqbal Qaiser's 1998 survey adds that Maharaja Ranjit Singh endowed the shrine with twenty-seven *ghumaon* of land and Rs 260, and that a fair was held here on the fifteenth of *Kattak Suddi*. In January 2019 a delegation of the Walled City of Lahore Authority, led by Director General Kamran Lashari, inspected the gurdwara together with the nearby Janam Asthan Mata Sahib Kaur and directed the local administration to restore both sites; that August, seventy-two years after Partition, the Evacuee Trust Property Board formally reopened Gurdwara Choa Sahib for worship, its chairman Dr Aamer Ahmed presiding over a ceremony open to Sikh pilgrims “whether they come from India or any other part of the world.”

## Bibliography
- Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (Punjabi History Board, 1998), p. 178.
- "WCLA to help restore Sikh sites in Jhelum," *Dawn*, 2 January 2019.
- "72 years after Partition, Pak opens Gurdwara Choa Sahib for Sikh devotees," *The Tribune* (Chandigarh), 2 August 2019.
- "A Complete Tour Guide To Ghurdwara Choa Sahib, Pakistan," Ministry of Religious Affairs and Interfaith Harmony, Government of Pakistan (text closely mirrors the English Wikipedia article "Gurdwara Chowa Sahib").
qa_note: Sources disagree on which gate of Rohtas Fort the gurdwara stands near: Iqbal Qaiser, *Historical Sikh Shrines in Pakistan* (1998), p. 178, places it “outside Kabuli Darwaza (gate),” while the Ministry of Religious Affairs and Interfaith Harmony's page (whose wording closely mirrors the English Wikipedia article and should be read as corroboration of the standard account rather than independent research) places it “near the fort's Talaqi gate” — the gate named in this entry's Description above. The two are not reconciled here.
